auth_facts.oauth_app_registration_requirement: For the OFFICIAL remote GitHub MCP server (https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/), GitHub-authored MCP host integrations (e.g. VS Code 1.101+) use a pre-registered OAuth flow with no separate app registration needed by the calling system - the one-click install buttons perform browser-based OAuth login on first use. A host application that is NOT one of GitHub's own pre-integrated clients must configure its OWN OAuth App or GitHub App to support remote OAuth per official docs ('Each MCP host application needs to configure a GitHub App or OAuth App to support remote access via OAuth'). PAT-based auth via the 'Authorization: Bearer <PAT>' header works with ANY host with no registration step.
auth_facts.fine_grained_pat_vs_installation_token_d: Fine-grained PATs are USER-scoped credentials: they act with the granting user's own permissions, are repository- or org-scoped (not enterprise-wide unless enterprise-owner-issued), carry an explicit expiration, and are subject to owner/org approval policies for org-owned resources. GitHub App installation access tokens are APP-scoped, generated server-side via the App's private key against a specific installation, are short-lived (~1 hour), and their permissions are the intersection of the App's declared permissions and what the installation was granted - they do NOT inherit a human user's personal permissions. The github-mcp-server README explicitly separates GitHub App user access tokens (delegated OAuth-App-like tokens tied to a human but issued via a GitHub App) from installation access tokens in its per-tool 'Fine-grained access tokens for X' sections - both are accepted for governance/branch-protection endpoints, but they are NOT the same credential class.
auth_facts.org_repo_scope_granularity: Fine-grained PATs are created against a specific resource owner (a user account or a single organization) and then scoped to 'all repositories' or a named subset of repositories owned by that account/org, each permission set independently (e.g. Contents:read+write, Administration:read, Pull requests:write) - granularity is per-repository-set x per-permission, unlike classic PATs' single-scope-string model (e.g. 'repo' grants blanket read/write across ALL repos the user can access). Org-owned resource fine-grained PATs may additionally require org admin APPROVAL before they become active, per official docs on organization personal access token policies.
auth_facts.sso_enforcement: For organizations that enforce SAML/OIDC SSO, both classic PATs and fine-grained PATs must be explicitly 'authorized' for that organization after creation (a separate authorization step in the token settings) before they can access that org's resources - an unauthorized token is not merely permission-limited but is refused outright for that org's resources until the holder completes SSO authorization. This applies uniformly to REST and GraphQL calls scoped to the enforcing org.
auth_facts.secondary_rate_limits: Per official docs (2026-09-14 snapshot): no more than 100 CONCURRENT requests (shared across REST+GraphQL); no more than 900 points/minute for REST endpoints and no more than 2,000 points/minute for the GraphQL endpoint; no more than 90 seconds of CPU time per 60 seconds of real time (of which at most 60s may be GraphQL); no more than 80 content-generating requests/minute and 500/hour (some endpoints lower); no more than 2,000 OAuth access-token requests/hour for GitHub Apps/OAuth Apps. Point costs: GraphQL non-mutation query=1pt, GraphQL mutation=5pts; REST GET/HEAD/OPTIONS=1pt, REST POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE=5pts (some REST endpoints carry an undisclosed different cost). Exceeding returns 403/429 with a secondary-limit message; if retry-after header present, wait that many seconds; otherwise wait >=1 minute with exponential backoff. There is NO way to check secondary rate limit status proactively (unlike primary limits, which are inspectable via response headers or GET /rate_limit).
auth_facts.primary_rate_limits: Unauthenticated: 60 req/hour (by source IP). Authenticated user (PAT, OAuth app token, GitHub App user token combined): 5,000 req/hour, or 15,000 req/hour if the acting App/OAuth App is owned/approved by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud org (note: a higher-limit app's usage still draws down the same shared 5,000 budget for the underlying PAT-based calls). GitHub App installation tokens: 5,000 req/hour minimum, scaling up to 12,500 req/hour cap based on installed repo count (+50/repo over 20) and org user count (+50/user over 20) if on a GitHub Enterprise Cloud org; 15,000 req/hour flat if the installation itself is on a GHE Cloud org. GITHUB_TOKEN in Actions: 1,000 req/hour/repository (15,000 for GHE Cloud-owned resources). GraphQL API has its own SEPARATE primary rate limit (point-based, not documented in the fetched REST page - tracked via the same /rate_limit resources.graphql bucket).
auth_facts.concurrency_limits: 100 concurrent requests max, shared across REST and GraphQL APIs for a given authenticated identity - this is the concurrency ceiling distinct from the per-minute point-based secondary limits.

scenario_preconditions.two_account_private_repo_isolation_test: Requires: (1) two distinct fine-grained PATs (or OAuth tokens) each minted for a DIFFERENT GitHub user account; (2) a target private repository owned by only ONE of the two accounts (or an org where only one account is a member/collaborator); (3) confirm via gh_get_diagnostics_actors_permissions_context (get_me) that each token resolves to the expected distinct login before the isolation assertion; (4) the non-authorized account's token must be verified to have NO collaborator/team grant on the repo (check gh_list_repository_collaborators or org membership) — otherwise a 'denied' result is not evidence of isolation, it is evidence of correctly-granted access; (5) expected result for the unauthorized token: 404 Not Found on gh_get_file_contents/get_repository_tree/pull_request_read (GitHub returns 404 rather than 403 for private-repo access-denial to avoid confirming repo existence to unauthorized callers) — a 403 instead of 404 should be treated as a signal worth investigating, not simply logged as pass/fail; (6) if SSO enforcement is active on the owning org, the token must ALSO be explicitly SSO-authorized for that org, or the isolation test will show a false negative (blocked for SSO reasons, not ownership reasons) — disambiguate via the token's own authorized-orgs listing before concluding the isolation succeeded for the right reason.
scenario_preconditions.branch_protection_rejection_test: Requires: (1) a target branch with EITHER legacy branch protection (verified via gh_get_branch_protection_legacy) OR an active repository ruleset (verified via gh_repository_ruleset_read) targeting that branch — critically, BOTH surfaces must be checked since GitHub allows them to coexist and either can independently block a merge; (2) a PR whose head does NOT satisfy at least one required condition (e.g., missing required approving review count, a required status check in pending/failing state, or require_last_push_approval unsatisfied because the last pusher was also the sole approver); (3) attempt gh_merge_pull_request and expect HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed with a body describing the specific unmet requirement — this is a DOCUMENTED GitHub behavior for protected-branch merge rejection distinct from a generic 403; (4) if enforce_admins/bypass_actors is configured and the calling identity is an admin/bypass actor, the merge may SUCCEED despite unmet conditions — the test must confirm the calling identity's role via gh_get_diagnostics_actors_permissions_context and exclude bypass-eligible identities to get a true rejection; (5) capture the exact 405 response body as evidence, since GitHub's message format documents which specific check failed.
scenario_preconditions.expired_sha_test: Requires: (1) obtain a valid commit SHA via gh_get_commit or gh_list_commits; (2) force the SHA to become unreachable — e.g. by force-pushing the branch to a different history (git push --force / rewriting refs) or by deleting the branch that was the SHA's sole reachability path, then waiting past GitHub's internal loose-object garbage collection window (GitHub does not document an exact GC delay, so tests should not assume immediate unreachability — a dangling commit can remain fetchable for some time via git protocol even after ref deletion); (3) call gh_get_commit or use the SHA as a base-SHA in gh_create_or_update_file/gh_merge_pull_request's expectedHeadSha; (4) expected result: 404 Not Found (or 422 Unprocessable Entity for the optimistic-concurrency 'sha' param on create_or_update_file/merge_pull_request/update_pull_request_branch, since a mismatched/stale SHA is documented to produce a conflict-class error there) — gap: the github-mcp-server tool docs do not explicitly state which of these two codes each write-path returns for a stale/expired SHA, so a real test run against a live sandbox repo is needed to pin the exact status code per tool before hardening a caller against it.
scenario_preconditions.revoked_installation_test: Requires: (1) a GitHub App installation on a test org/repo, authenticated calls made successfully first to establish baseline via gh_get_diagnostics_actors_permissions_context; (2) an org/repo admin revokes the App's installation (Settings > Integrations > GitHub Apps > Configure > Uninstall) OR the installation access token is allowed to expire (~1 hour lifetime per official docs) without renewal; (3) subsequent API calls using the now-invalid installation token are EXPECTED to return 401 Unauthorized (token invalid/expired) rather than 403 (403 implies a recognized-but-insufficiently-permissioned identity, which is a different failure class); (4) if using the remote MCP server's OAuth flow rather than a raw installation token, expect the MCP session's next tool call to surface an authentication-refresh failure — the official docs do not document the exact remote-MCP-server error shape returned to an MCP client in this case, which is a genuine DOCUMENTATION GAP for this scenario; (5) recovery path is always re-authentication (new OAuth flow or new installation token mint), never a retry of the same call.
scenario_preconditions.write_then_read_back_test: Requires: (1) perform a write op with a documented response body containing the authoritative new state (e.g. gh_create_or_update_file returns the new commit+content sha; gh_issue_write:create returns the created issue with its number; gh_create_pull_request returns the new PR object) — prefer asserting against THIS returned object first, since it is the most current representation with zero replication lag; (2) THEN perform an independent read (gh_get_file_contents with the new sha/ref, gh_issue_read:get with the new issue_number, gh_pull_request_read:get with the new pullNumber) and diff against the write response; (3) GitHub's REST API is documented as strongly consistent for a given resource after a successful write (no documented eventual-consistency window for repo contents/issues/PRs in the fetched official docs), BUT secondary indexes used by SEARCH endpoints (gh_search_code, gh_search_issues, gh_search_pull_requests, gh_search_commits) ARE independently documented to lag behind live writes — a write-then-immediately-search assertion is NOT a valid consistency test and will produce false negatives; use direct get/read tools for the read-back leg, not search tools; (4) for gh_create_or_update_file specifically, the immediately-prior blob 'sha' becomes the required input for the NEXT write to the same path — capture it from the write response rather than re-reading, to avoid an unnecessary extra call and to sidestep any read-after-write timing question entirely.

contradictions: The MCP tool catalog (github-mcp-server README, 'governance' toolset) documents ONLY the newer repository-rulesets API surface, while the separate REST API docs (docs.github.com/en/rest/branches/branch-protection) document a parallel, older 'legacy branch protection' surface (branches/{branch}/protection and its many sub-resources). Both surfaces can be independently active on the same branch simultaneously and can each independently block a merge. Neither official source documents how the two interact when both apply conflicting requirements (e.g., legacy protection requires 1 approval while a ruleset requires 2) - this is a genuine ambiguity in official documentation, not resolved by either doc reviewed.

Within the github-mcp-server tool catalog itself, PR review-comment identifiers are inconsistently typed across tools in the same toolset: add_reply_to_pull_request_comment takes a NUMERIC id (from a #discussion_r... URL anchor), while pull_request_review_write's resolve_thread/unresolve_thread methods require a GraphQL node ID (PRRT_...) obtainable only via pull_request_read:get_review_comments. A caller must know which identifier space a given write tool expects; the README does not cross-reference this.

Pagination style is inconsistent across the MCP tool catalog: most REST-backed tools use numeric page/perPage; a subset of GraphQL-backed tools (list_issues, get_discussion_comments, get_review_comments) use cursor-based 'after' pagination instead. A generic connector abstraction cannot assume one pagination contract across all read operations.

create_or_update_file exposes an explicit optimistic-concurrency 'sha' (base-SHA) parameter for update-in-place safety, but the multi-file push_files tool and the delete_file tool document NO equivalent expected-current-state parameter, despite being equally capable of clobbering concurrent changes. This is an asymmetry in the official tool schema, not merely a documentation omission judgment call.

The REST branch-protection docs explicitly mark the 'contexts' field on required_status_checks as a 'Closing down notice' (deprecated) in favor of 'checks[]' with app_id binding, yet the field remains present and functional in both the Get and Update endpoints as of the 2026-09-14 snapshot - a caller integrating today must decide whether to write against the deprecated-but-live field or the current field, and the docs do not state a removal date.
gaps: No official GHES (GitHub Enterprise Server) support for the remote MCP server (https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/) was found: the official docs state remote hosting is not available for GHES, and Enterprise Server customers must use the LOCAL github-mcp-server binary/Docker image pointed at their GHES hostname via --gh-host/GITHUB_HOST instead. This connector catalog's 'endpoint' fields describe the github.com-hosted remote MCP server; a GHES deployment changes the base URL and requires local hosting.

The exact HTTP status code returned by create_or_update_file / merge_pull_request / update_pull_request_branch for a STALE or EXPIRED sha/expectedHeadSha is not explicitly pinned in the fetched official tool docs (only that the parameter exists for concurrency control) - confirmed by direct doc text as ambiguous between 404/409/422 depending on tool; would require a live sandbox call to pin definitively.

GraphQL API's own separate primary rate limit (point-based cost model) was referenced by the REST rate-limit doc but its full point-cost table was not fetched in this research pass (only the REST-side secondary-limit GraphQL point costs of 1/5 per query/mutation were retrieved) - a complete picture of GraphQL primary limits was not verified against docs.github.com/en/graphql/overview/rate-limits-and-query-limits-for-the-graphql-api in this session.

The remote MCP server's exact error response SHAPE (JSON-RPC error code/message format) for an expired/revoked OAuth token or GitHub App installation was not found in the fetched docs - remote-server.md documents toolsets, headers, and insiders mode, but not its authentication-failure error contract, leaving the 'revoked_installation_test' scenario's expected-response assertion partially unverified against official sources.

Whether the OFFICIAL remote MCP server enforces the SAME secondary/concurrency rate limits as raw REST/GraphQL API calls, or applies an additional MCP-specific throttling layer on top, is not documented in either remote-server.md or the general REST rate-limit docs - this is an open question for any capacity-planning use of the connector at scale.

list_issues, get_discussion_comments and get_review_comments are GraphQL-backed per their cursor-pagination style, but the README does not explicitly disclose which underlying transport (REST vs GraphQL) backs EACH individual tool - this was inferred from the pagination parameter shape (page number vs cursor 'after') rather than stated directly by GitHub, and should be treated as a moderate-confidence inference, not a confirmed fact, for tools not explicitly marked.

This research relied on live web fetches of github.com and docs.github.com pages successfully retrieved during this session (as of stated observed_at 2026-09-14); no access limitation was encountered, so no source in this catalog is based on offline/training-data recall - all citations trace to the fetched snapshot_ref URLs.

auth_facts.minimal_scope_per_capability_principle: Google explicitly instructs requesting the narrowest scope per feature rather than one blanket grant — e.g. gmail.readonly alone for search/get/history/list, gmail.send (not modify) if the connector only ever sends, gmail.labels alone for label CRUD without message content access, gmail.compose for draft management without full inbox read/modify.
auth_facts.https://mail.google.com/ note: Explicitly documented as the ONLY scope required for immediate, permanent (trash-bypassing) delete of threads/messages; all other operations (including regular trash/untrash) work under gmail.modify. Connectors should avoid requesting this scope unless permanent bypass-trash delete is a genuine requirement.
auth_facts.domain_wide_delegation_vs_user_oauth: Two distinct auth models: (1) standard user-consent OAuth2 — a human explicitly grants scopes via consent screen, works for any Gmail/Workspace account, connector acts strictly as that user; (2) service-account + domain-wide delegation — a Workspace super-admin authorizes a service account's client ID in the Admin Console to impersonate any/all users in the domain without per-user consent, used for admin-managed integrations (backup, DLP, org-wide automation). Domain-wide delegation is a Google Workspace-only capability; it is NOT available on consumer/personal Gmail accounts (no Admin Console). gmail.settings.sharing explicitly documented as restricted to 'a service account with domain-wide delegation' — administrative-only regardless of consent scope.
auth_facts.oauth_verification_tiers: Non-sensitive scopes need only basic OAuth app verification. Sensitive and Restricted scopes require Google's additional verification process (CASA/security assessment for Restricted scopes storing or transmitting the data); an unverified public app shows an 'unverified app' warning to end users until this completes.

scenario_preconditions.send: Caller must hold gmail.send/compose/mail.google.com scope AND the From address in the raw MIME message must be either the primary address or a verified send-as alias (see settings.sendAs.list) — sending as an unverified alias is expected to fail (exact error not reconfirmed this session).
scenario_preconditions.reply_forward: Requires prior read access (gmail.readonly or broader) to fetch the original message's headers/attachments before composing the reply/forward payload for send.
scenario_preconditions.history_sync: Caller must already possess a previously-stored historyId (from getProfile, messages.get, or a prior history.list call) to request incremental sync; first-ever sync for a mailbox has no historyId and must instead perform a full sync via messages.list + batched messages.get.
scenario_preconditions.batch_label_workspace_classification: Classification Label values (as opposed to plain labelIds) require a Google Workspace account; consumer Gmail accounts do not support this field and it should be omitted/ignored for those accounts.
scenario_preconditions.domain_wide_delegation_setup: Requires a Workspace super-admin to pre-authorize the service account's OAuth client ID + specific scope set in the Admin Console (Security > API Controls > Domain-wide Delegation) before any impersonated call succeeds; this is an out-of-band admin action the connector cannot perform itself.

Official Gmail API sync guide (fetched 2026-09-14, page last-updated banner shows 2026-09-10 UTC) explicitly states the response is HTTP 404 Not Found, with the required recovery being a full resync. auth_facts.minimal_scope_per_capability_principle: Google explicitly recommends drive.file over drive/drive.readonly wherever possible: drive.file only grants access to files the app itself created OR that the user explicitly opened/selected via the app's own picker UI or the Google Picker API — NOT the user's entire Drive. This is the officially-recommended 'non-sensitive' default for connectors that don't need whole-Drive search/read. A connector needing full 'search all my files' or 'read any file the user can see' behavior must request the Restricted drive or drive.readonly scope instead, which triggers additional OAuth verification (and, if data is stored/transmitted server-side, a security assessment).
auth_facts.restricted_scope_qualification: Only apps in specific categories (Backup and sync; Productivity and education; Reporting and security) qualify to use Restricted Drive scopes at all per Google's stated policy; apps outside those categories are expected to use drive.file + Picker instead.
auth_facts.domain_wide_delegation_vs_user_oauth: Same two-model distinction as Gmail: standard user-consent OAuth2 (per-user grant, works on any Google account) vs. service-account + domain-wide delegation (Workspace admin pre-authorizes a service account to impersonate users domain-wide without per-user consent; Workspace-only, requires Admin Console configuration, not available on consumer Drive accounts).
auth_facts.shared_drive_admin_bypass: useDomainAdminAccess parameter (seen on drives.list/permissions endpoints) allows a Workspace super-admin to view/manage Shared Drive metadata/permissions across the whole domain without being a member of every drive — an admin-only escalation path distinct from normal per-file/per-drive access grants.

scenario_preconditions.shared_drive_visibility: Any files.list/search call that should include Shared Drive items MUST set BOTH supportsAllDrives=true and includeItemsFromAllDrives=true; omitting either silently scopes the search to My Drive only. This is the single most common Shared Drive integration pitfall.
scenario_preconditions.native_vs_binary_content_routing: Before attempting to read a file's bytes, the connector MUST branch on File.mimeType: if it starts with 'application/vnd.google-apps.' (except '...folder' and '...shortcut', which have no content at all) the connector MUST call files.export with an explicit target mimeType; for any other MIME type, files.get?alt=media (download) is used instead. Calling download on a native type, or export on a binary type, is expected to fail.
scenario_preconditions.shortcut_resolution: Before any content operation, the connector MUST check whether File.mimeType == 'application/vnd.google-apps.shortcut'; if so, it must re-resolve via shortcutDetails.targetId (a second files.get call) to reach the real, content-bearing file.
scenario_preconditions.resumable_upload_session_reuse: A resumable session URI is valid for exactly one week of inactivity; a connector queuing large uploads for later must not persist and reuse a session URI beyond that window — it must restart the initiation step.
scenario_preconditions.safe_retry_of_creates: Any create/upload/copy operation that must be safely retried after an ambiguous network failure should first call files.generateIds to obtain a pre-allocated ID and pass it explicitly; Google guarantees a retried create with the same pre-generated ID returns HTTP 409 Conflict instead of duplicating the file. Without a pre-generated ID, retries silently create duplicates — no other dedupe mechanism exists.
scenario_preconditions.ssrf_risk_flag: Because Drive API v3 has NO native URL-fetch/upload-by-URL primitive (see drive.files.upload_by_url), any connector-level 'create file from URL' feature necessarily performs its OWN outbound HTTP fetch of a caller-supplied URL server-side before uploading the bytes to Drive. This is a textbook SSRF vector: the URL is attacker/user-controlled, the fetch happens from the connector's server-side network context, and a naive implementation could be used to probe internal network ranges, cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254), or other services reachable from that host. Mitigations (not Google-documented, general SSRF hygiene the connector must implement itself): allowlist/denylist scheme+host, resolve and block private/loopback/link-local IP ranges before connecting, disable redirects or re-validate the destination of each redirect hop, enforce a response size/time cap, and run the fetch from an egress-restricted network segment.

contradictions: v2 vs v3 API shape: Drive API v2 exposed dedicated files.trash/files.untrash verbs (confirmed present in the fetched v2 REST resource tree); v3 removed them in favor of PATCHing the boolean File.trashed field via the general files.update method. A connector or migration guide written against v2 assumptions about a dedicated trash endpoint will be wrong for v3.

auth_facts: Delegated vs application grants are fully independent; application permission Sites.Read.All lets an app read ALL sites in the tenant without a signed-in user (subject to admin consent), while Sites.Selected restricts app-only access to explicitly configured site collections.

Sites.Selected is the recommended minimal-blast-radius application permission; the specific site collections and permission level (read/write) are configured out-of-band in SharePoint Online admin settings, not via the Graph consent screen alone.

A KB whose data was ingested by an admin identity must still be queried using the QUERYING USER's own delegated permission at query time — an application-permission ingestion path does not grant that same access to end-user query-time reads; mixing admin-ingested content with user-scoped query needs a delegated-permission read path or an equivalent app-enforced ACL check, which Graph itself does not automatically provide.
scenario_preconditions: For >=250MB file upload/update: must use createUploadSession (resumable), never a single PUT.

For typed custom columns (lookup, person, group, multi-value): use $expand=fields and interpret the fields facet's LookupId/LookupValue, and multi-value arrays per column type; null represents an empty/cleared field.
ETag concurrency: always read current eTag before PATCH/DELETE to avoid 412 errors on list items.
contradictions: Site resource is documented as read-only ('no ability to create new sites') at the resource-overview level, yet Sites.Create.All / Sites.Create (delegated) permission entries exist in the permissions reference allowing site collection creation — site collection creation is a separate, narrower capability from general Site CRUD.
gaps: No official Graph API to create a net-new SharePoint site via the /sites resource path directly (site creation is handled through Sites.Create permission via a different endpoint family, not detailed in the sharepoint.md overview).

Exact behavior of concurrent query-time ACL enforcement for admin-ingested vs user-queried KB content is not explicitly documented as a single unified Graph capability; must be implemented at the calling application's authorization layer.

auth_facts: Application-permission calls CANNOT use the /me shortcut; they must target /users/{id} explicitly — /me only resolves in a delegated (signed-in user) context.

Primary mailbox access is via /users/{id}; shared mailbox access uses the same message/event resource model but is reached via the shared mailbox's own address as {id}, with admins optionally scoping app-only access to specific shared mailboxes via application access policy.

SendAs and SendOnBehalf are modeled via the 'from' and 'sender' properties on the message resource, not via distinct permission scopes — the delegate relationship must be pre-configured in Exchange, and Mail.Send governs whether the app can perform the send at all.

Administrators can configure an application access policy to restrict an app-only Mail.*/Calendars.*/MailboxSettings.* grant to a specific subset of mailboxes rather than tenant-wide, even though the OAuth application permission itself is tenant-wide by default.

A meeting invite (event with attendees) always triggers 'external_send' effect because Exchange automatically emails invite/update/cancellation notices to attendees; this is not a separate explicit 'send' call.
scenario_preconditions: Application-permission access to online meetings requires an admin-configured application access policy binding the app to specific user IDs (confirmed via application-post-onlinemeetings doc).

A 202/201 accepted response for sendMail, reply, forward, or event creation with attendees is NOT proof of external delivery; delivery confirmation requires separate mechanisms (e.g., message trace) not part of these APIs.
conversationId groups related messages across a thread; MIME content access uses a distinct $value endpoint (GET /messages/{id}/$value) requiring the same Mail.Read* permission.

Recurring event occurrences are individually addressable once expanded via calendarView or the 'instances' relationship; timezone must be explicit per event via the start/end TimeZone property or via Prefer: outlook.timezone header for response formatting.
contradictions: findMeetingTimes documentation states no application-permission support at all, which contradicts a naive assumption that any Graph read operation can be run app-only with a tenant-wide grant — this operation is delegated (work/school) ONLY.
gaps: Exact DST-crossing behavior for recurring events (a series whose pattern crosses a spring-forward/fall-back boundary) is not explicitly detailed in the top-level docs fetched; requires deeper reading of the event/recurrencePattern resource pages.
No official delivery-receipt or bounce-notification API is exposed by Microsoft Graph for sendMail; asserting delivery requires external tooling not covered by this catalog.

auth_facts: CONFIRMED: RSC (resource-specific-consent) is a DISTINCT authorization framework from standard tenant-wide Team.*/Channel.*/Chat.* Graph permissions. RSC lets a resource owner (team owner, chat member, or meeting organizer/presenter) grant an app access scoped to ONE instance of a resource (one team, one chat) rather than tenant-wide.

RSC has two access modes matching standard Graph: 'Application context RSC' (app accesses data without a signed-in user, consented by resource owner at install time) and 'Delegated context RSC' (app accesses data only in the context of a signed-in user's own session).

CRITICAL: do not conflate migration-only/restricted RSC permissions with normal messaging permissions. Some RSC entries (e.g., ChannelMeetingAudioVideo.Stream.Group, LiveShareSession.ReadWrite.Group) are Delegated-only with NO Application form, while others like ChannelMessage.Read.Group/ChannelMessage.Send.Group are Application-only with NO Delegated RSC form — the split is asymmetric per permission, not a simple both-or-neither pattern.

ChannelMember.Read.Group and ChannelMember.ReadWrite.Group RSC entries show 'NA' for BOTH Delegated and Application — meaning channel membership management is NOT exposed via RSC at all under Teams; it must go through the standard tenant-wide ChannelMember.*.All permissions instead.

TeamsActivity.Send RSC application permission is always enabled at the tenant level and does not require admin consent for that specific low-risk 'Basic RSC Permission' category; this is an explicit exception to the general RSC consent requirement.
scenario_preconditions: Online meeting creation via application permission requires BOTH the OnlineMeetings.ReadWrite.All grant AND a separate tenant-admin-configured application access policy binding the app to the specific target userId — the permission grant alone is documented as insufficient.

Standalone online meetings (created via POST /onlineMeetings) are NOT calendar-backed and do NOT support later transcript retrieval; calendar-backed meetings (created via the Events API with isOnlineMeeting=true) are required for transcript-capable meetings.

Polling for new Teams resources must not exceed once-per-day per the documented polling requirements (except teamsAsyncOperation, which is designed for frequent polling); violating this classifies the app as being in breach of the Microsoft APIs Terms of Use and risks throttling/suspension.
contradictions: ChannelMessage.Send and ChannelMessage.ReadWrite show NO application-permission column populated in the standard permissions reference, meaning channel message sending is delegated-only at the tenant-wide-permission level — but the RSC framework DOES expose ChannelMessage.Send.Group and ChannelMessage.Read.Group as APPLICATION-ONLY (not delegated) resource-scoped equivalents. A caller must use RSC, not the tenant-wide permission, to send channel messages app-only.

The task instruction to 'distinguish application vs delegated vs RSC permission scoping precisely' is directly supported by finding that the two frameworks are NOT interchangeable and in fact invert which mode (delegated vs application) is available for the same conceptual action (e.g., channel messaging) depending on which framework is used.
gaps: Exact shared-channel (cross-tenant) membership constraints for ChannelMember.ReadWrite.All were not detailed on the fetched pages and would require the dedicated shared-channels documentation.

RSC 'Basic RSC Permissions' auto-consent list is limited to only the three TeamsActivity.Send.* entries per the fetched page; whether other permissions have been added to this always-on list since would need a live re-check.

auth_facts: Excel-on-Graph shares the SAME Files.* permission scopes as OneDrive/SharePoint (Files.Read, Files.ReadWrite, Files.Read.All, Files.ReadWrite.All) — there is no Excel-specific OAuth scope; access control is governed entirely by the underlying drive's Files.*/Sites.* permissions.

All API calls to the Excel resource require ONLY Files.Read (read actions) or Files.ReadWrite (read+write actions) at minimum per the doc's explicit 'Authorization and scopes' section — no separate Excel.* scope family exists.
scenario_preconditions: CONFIRMED explicitly: 'Support for workbooks stored in OneDrive Consumer platform is still not available. At this time, only the files stored in business platform are supported by Excel REST APIs.' — personal Microsoft account OneDrive files CANNOT be operated on via the Excel Graph API regardless of auth mode; only OneDrive for Business, SharePoint, or Group drives are supported.

Workbook session semantics: (1) Persistent session (persistChanges=true) — most efficient/performant, changes saved, expires after ~5 min inactivity; (2) Non-persistent session (persistChanges=false) — changes NOT saved to source, held in a temporary server-side copy, expires after ~7 min inactivity, useful for analysis without mutating the document; (3) Sessionless (no workbook-session-id header) — works but inefficient (server re-locates the workbook copy each call) AND changes made without a session ARE persisted by default, which is a notable behavior a caller relying on 'no session = safe/read-only' would get wrong.

On session expiry (404 on the session id), the caller must either create a new session and continue, or proactively refresh/keep-alive the session on a periodic cadence before expiry — this is the documented sequential recovery path; there is no automatic session renewal.

429 Too Many Requests handling and exact Retry-After semantics were not detailed on the fetched excel-concept-overview page itself; this is a documented gap requiring the dedicated throttling reference page.
contradictions: The Excel session model's default behavior for a sessionless call ('changes ARE persisted') can contradict an integrator's intuitive assumption that omitting a session header defaults to a safe, non-mutating mode; the doc explicitly warns against this assumption.
gaps: No explicit numeric 429/Retry-After behavior or backoff guidance was present on the fetched excel-concept-overview page; the task's request for '429+Retry-After, sequential recovery' detail beyond the session-expiry (404) recovery path could not be fully verified from this specific page and would need the dedicated Graph throttling documentation.
No hard 'Large Range' size threshold (cell count or payload byte size) is documented; only qualitative guidance to split large ranges into smaller read/write calls.

Exclusive-lock behavior beyond the persistent/non-persistent/sessionless session model (e.g., whether two concurrent persistent sessions on the same workbook can conflict) was not explicitly detailed on the fetched page.

auth_facts.http_200_ok_false_shape: Every Slack Web API response returns HTTP 200 on the transport layer REGARDLESS of application-level success. The actual success/failure signal is exclusively the top-level 'ok' boolean field in the JSON body; ok:false is accompanied by an 'error' string field (and sometimes 'warning'/'response_metadata.warnings'). A caller that checks only the HTTP status code will incorrectly treat every application-level failure as a success. This applies uniformly across chat.*, conversations.*, files.*, users.*, usergroups.*, reactions.*, search.*, reminders.*, team.info, auth.test.
auth_facts.events_api_signature_verification: Every incoming Events API HTTP POST to Kiro Crew's registered request URL must be verified using Slack's signing secret: compute an HMAC-SHA256 over the string 'v0:{X-Slack-Request-Timestamp}:{raw_request_body}' using the app's signing secret, base64/hex-encode per Slack's documented format as 'v0={signature}', and compare in constant time against the 'X-Slack-Signature' header. The 'X-Slack-Request-Timestamp' header must also be checked against current time (Slack documents rejecting requests older than roughly 5 minutes) to guard against replay of a captured, validly-signed request. This verification must occur BEFORE any Kiro Crew business logic reads the payload as trusted.
auth_facts.events_api_replay_dedupe: Slack's Events API can and does redeliver the same event (e.g. on a slow/ambiguous HTTP response from the receiver, or retry-on-timeout behavior), each redelivery carrying an X-Slack-Retry-Num header and the same underlying event_id inside the JSON body. Kiro Crew must deduplicate on event_id (or a combination of event_id plus event_time) with a durable idempotency store, since signature verification alone does not prevent legitimate re-delivery from being double-processed.
auth_facts.self_loop_risk: A bot posting into a channel it is also listening to via Events API (e.g. message.channels) will receive its OWN posted message as an incoming event. Slack's message payload includes a 'bot_id' field (and for the newer subtype, a 'subtype':'bot_message' or the bot_profile object) that Kiro Crew MUST check against its own known bot_id (obtainable via auth.test) to short-circuit and ignore self-authored events; failing to do so risks an infinite reply loop where the bot keeps responding to its own output.
auth_facts.inbound_channel_binding_trust: The channel/team/user identifiers found INSIDE an inbound Events API payload must never be trusted purely because the JSON claims them. The only trusted binding mechanism is: (1) verified request signature (proves the payload came from Slack's servers for THIS app's signing secret), combined with (2) the team_id/enterprise_id in the verified payload being cross-checked against Kiro Crew's own record of which workspace/org installed this app (from the OAuth install record), and (3) using auth.test or the OAuth access response's own returned identity fields as the authoritative source for 'who am I' rather than any self-reported identity elsewhini a message payload. Self-reported message identity fields alone (e.g. a 'user' or 'username' string in a spoofable legacy webhook-style payload) must never be used as the sole basis for a trust/authorization decision.
auth_facts.rate_limit_tiers: Slack's Web API documents four general Tier rate limit buckets for token-bucket-limited methods (Tier 1 = most restrictive, roughly 1 request/minute historically documented for some legacy heavy methods; Tier 2 ~20 requests/minute; Tier 3 ~50 requests/minute; Tier 4 ~100+ requests/minute), applied per-method and generally per-workspace/per-app-token combination. chat.postMessage additionally has its OWN special-cased, per-channel short-burst limit (roughly documented historically as about 1 message per second sustained per channel, with short bursts tolerated) that is DISTINCT from and layered on top of the general Tier system. Enterprise Grid and paid-plan workspaces may have different absolute Tier ceilings than free-plan workspaces per Slack's rate-limit documentation; exact current numeric ceilings per tier and per plan should be re-verified live against https://api.slack.com/apis/rate-limits at this exact snapshot date rather than assumed frozen, since Slack has adjusted specific tier ceilings across past documentation revisions.
auth_facts.token_type_summary: Three broad auth modes recur across nearly all operations above: (1) bot_token (xoxb-, installed per-workspace or per-org, acts as the app/bot's own identity, most common and generally the recommended default for Kiro Crew), (2) user_token (xoxp-, acts as the authorizing human's own identity, REQUIRED for the search.* family and generally preferred for reminders.* and self-profile users.profile.set), (3) org_app_token (relevant only in Enterprise Grid org-wide app installs, where a single org-level installation can act across multiple member workspaces; individual API calls still typically resolve to a bot_token-shaped credential scoped by an explicit team_id parameter rather than a wholly separate token TYPE for most listed methods -- org-wide apps do not introduce a fourth distinct calling convention for the operations covered here, they mainly add the team_id disambiguation parameter).

search.messages / search.files / search.all are strictly user-token-only methods with NO bot-token support; this basic history/keyword search backend must not be conflated with Slack's higher-tier advanced/enterprise/'context' or AI-assisted search product surfaces, which sit behind separate plan-level entitlement and are not simply 'the same API with a higher rate limit' -- they are a distinct capability boundary not fully enumerated in the plain method reference pages.

Pagination model is NOT uniform across the platform: conversations.* (history, replies, members, list), users.list, and files.getUploadURLExternal-adjacent list-style methods use cursor-based response_metadata.next_cursor; files.list documents BOTH a legacy numeric page/paging field and a cursor field simultaneously (dual/ambiguous); search.messages/search.files/search.all use legacy numeric page/count pagination with NO cursor; usergroups.list documents no pagination mechanism at all (single full-list response). Treat 'Slack uses cursor pagination' as true only for a SUBSET of methods, not a platform-wide guarantee.

reminders.add / reminders.list bot-token eligibility is ambiguous/under-specified relative to the rest of the Web API surface (most of which cleanly separates bot vs user token support); this should be treated as an open verification item rather than asserted confidently in either direction at this snapshot.

HTTP transport-level success (200 OK) is DECOUPLED from application-level success across literally every method listed; conflating the two is a documented, platform-wide contradiction risk for any naive integration.

mcp_transport.current: Streamable HTTP. The V2 MCP server is generally available at https://mcp.asana.com/v2/mcp and explicitly documented as using Streamable HTTP transport (docs/using-asanas-mcp-server: 'Ensure your client supports OAuth authentication and Streamable HTTP transport'; docs/connecting-mcp-clients-to-asanas-v2-server confirms the same URL across all client setup instructions).
mcp_transport.retired_or_deprecated: The V1 Beta MCP server at https://mcp.asana.com/sse is an SSE-based transport and is explicitly marked DEPRECATED, shutting down 2026-08-05 (extended from an earlier 2026-05-11 date per docs/integrating-with-asanas-mcp-server; a couple of other pages fetched in this session still show the pre-extension 05/11/2026 date, e.g. docs/using-asanas-mcp-server and docs/connecting-mcp-clients-to-asanas-v2-server -- this is an internal documentation inconsistency on Asana's own site, flagged under contradictions below). As of the 2026-09-14 research date, the V1/SSE endpoint should be treated as retiring/retired, not as a currently supported production transport, and Streamable HTTP v2 is the current, authoritative transport.
mcp_transport.explicit_confirmation: Confirmed directly from official docs, not inferred: 'The V2 MCP server is generally available and uses OAuth for authorization' (integrating-with-asanas-mcp-server) and 'The V1 Beta MCP server https://mcp.asana.com/sse is deprecated and will shut down' (same page).

registration_model.mcp_server_auth: Requires PRE-REGISTRATION of an OAuth app in the Asana developer console ('MCP app' type) to obtain a client_id/client_secret. Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) is explicitly NOT supported: 'Although these documents can be used to dynamically discover endpoints, clients must still pre-register to get a client id and client secret as described above. Dynamic client registration is not supported with Asana's V2 MCP Server.' (docs/integrating-with-asanas-mcp-server, 'Discovery endpoint' section). A discovery document IS published at https://mcp.asana.com/v2/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource pointing to https://app.asana.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, but discovery does not substitute for pre-registration.
registration_model.native_oauth_app_model: SEPARATE and DISTINCT surface: standard Asana API OAuth apps (for REST API access) are also created in the same developer console but as a different app TYPE ('standard API app' vs 'MCP app'). Tokens are NOT interchangeable: 'Tokens issued for MCP apps only work with the MCP server. This separation follows MCP security best practices -- if a token is compromised, the blast radius is contained. If you need to make standard Asana API requests, create a separate API app and obtain tokens through the standard OAuth or PAT flow.' (docs/integrating-with-asanas-mcp-server, and reconfirmed in docs/mcp-tools-reference 'Tips for developers': 'MCP tokens do not work with the Asana REST API... For standard API access, create a separate app and authenticate through the standard OAuth flow.')
registration_model.scopes_model_difference: Native OAuth apps use fine-grained resource:action scopes (documented exhaustively in docs/oauth-scopes, e.g. tasks:read, projects:write, attachments:delete, etc.) following least-privilege. MCP apps use NO discrete scopes at all: 'MCP apps in Asana do not use permission scopes. When a user authorizes an MCP client, the token automatically requests full access to all available tools... Access is determined by the authenticated user's Asana permissions.' (docs/mcp-tools-reference, 'Access and permissions'). Including a scope parameter in an MCP OAuth authorization request produces an explicit error ('Invalid scope(s) requested') per docs/integrating-with-asanas-mcp-server troubleshooting section -- omit scope entirely or pass 'default'.
registration_model.authorization_endpoint_distinction: MCP authorization reuses Asana's standard OAuth authorize endpoint (https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_authorize) but adds an OPTIONAL resource parameter (resource=https://mcp.asana.com/v2) to target the MCP server specifically; this is the only structural difference in the authorization request itself between the two surfaces.
registration_model.token_lifetime: MCP access tokens expire after 1 hour; refresh tokens follow the same refresh-token grant flow documented for standard Asana OAuth (docs/integrating-with-asanas-mcp-server, 'Refresh tokens').

workspace_scoping.fact: MCP tokens are workspace-scoped AT AUTHORIZATION TIME: 'When you authorize an MCP session, you select a specific workspace. All tool calls in that session are scoped to that workspace. To work across multiple workspaces, you need separate sessions.' (docs/mcp-tools-reference, 'Tips for developers'). This differs from a standard Asana OAuth/PAT token, which is not pinned to a single workspace and can address any workspace the authenticated user belongs to, subject to a workspace_gid path/query parameter per request.

gid_addressing.fact: Asana's entire API addresses resources by GID (Globally unique IDentifier) -- confirmed consistently across every fetched endpoint (workspace_gid, project_gid, task_gid, user_gid, team_gid, custom_field_gid, etc.) in the REST API Reference sidebar and individual endpoint pages (e.g. reference/getTask, reference/getworkspaceevents). GIDs are opaque numeric-string identifiers; the 'me' string is a special-cased alias accepted specifically by user-related endpoints/tools (get_user, GET /users/{user_gid}) as a shortcut for the authenticated user, not a general GID substitute elsewhere.

date_vs_datetime.fact: Confirmed explicitly in docs/dates-and-times: date-ONLY fields (e.g. a task's due_on) use ISO 8601 date format YYYY-MM-DD with no time/timezone component. Date-AND-TIME fields (e.g. created_at, or a task's due_at) use full ISO 8601 datetime format YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.fffZ (UTC, 'Z' suffix, 3-digit fractional seconds). Tasks in Asana support EITHER a due_on (date-only, no specific time) OR a due_at (specific date+time) -- these are documented as distinct, mutually-relevant fields on the task object, not interchangeable representations of one concept. Query parameters that accept a date/time (e.g. modified_since on GET /tasks) require the full datetime format even when semantically day-level.

Applies to REST custom_fields/custom_field_settings endpoints and to any MCP tool value depending on them (create_tasks/update_tasks custom field values).

mcp_tool_taxonomy.interactive_tools_caveat: Interactive/preview tools render a confirmation UI only in two specific named third-party MCP client products, not universally across all MCP clients; 'Other MCP clients use the standard write tools directly' (docs/mcp-tools-reference) -- meaning a client like Kiro Crew connecting to the same MCP server would invoke create_tasks/create_project/search_tasks directly with no built-in confirmation step, unless Kiro Crew itself implements an equivalent confirmation layer.
mcp_tool_taxonomy.migration_note_v1_to_v2: Tool names in V2 dropped the 'asana_' prefix used in V1 (e.g. asana_create_task -> create_task). Many V1 tools required an explicit workspaceGid parameter; in V2 this is no longer needed because workspace scope is now fixed at OAuth authorization time.
mcp_tool_taxonomy.authoritative_schema_source: Asana explicitly and repeatedly states that this documentation page is NOT the authoritative source for tool parameter schemas -- the live 'tools/list' MCP command is: 'Tool parameters may change over time. The authoritative source for parameter names, types, and constraints is the tools/list MCP command, not this page.' This is a structural caveat applying to every operation in the 'operations' array above that is sourced from the MCP Tools Reference page.

real_task_create_complete_reopen_cycle.steps: 1) create_tasks / POST /tasks with a workspace or project context. 2) update_tasks / PUT /tasks/{gid} with completed:true to complete. 3) update_tasks / PUT /tasks/{gid} with completed:false to reopen.
real_task_create_complete_reopen_cycle.preconditions: Authenticated session (MCP: workspace-scoped OAuth token; REST: PAT or OAuth token with tasks:write) with create+edit permission in the target project/workspace. No official 'reopen' verb exists distinct from setting completed:false -- confirmed via updatetask reference (completed is a plain boolean field, not a state machine with named transitions).
real_task_create_complete_reopen_cycle.verification: Read back via get_task/GET /tasks/{gid} after each step and check the completed and completed_at fields; completed_at is expected to populate on completion and clear (null) on reopen, though the exact null-on-reopen behavior for completed_at was not independently re-confirmed on the fetched getTask/updatetask pages this session -- flagged as a gap.
real_task_create_complete_reopen_cycle.risk: Completion/reopen actions are auto-logged by Asana as stories; MCP add_comment explicitly warns not to duplicate this via a manual comment, confirming the system already produces an audit trail for this transition (docs/mcp-tools-reference).

permission_shrink_test.scenario: A user's Asana permissions are reduced (e.g. removed from a project or demoted) WHILE an MCP or OAuth token issued under their prior permission state is still valid (tokens last up to 1 hour for MCP before requiring refresh).
permission_shrink_test.expected_behavior_per_docs: MCP Tools Reference states access is determined dynamically by 'the authenticated user's Asana permissions' at call time, not cached at authorization time: 'they can only access workspaces, projects, and tasks they already have access to' (present tense, implying live permission check). This suggests a permission shrink should take effect on the NEXT tool call, not just at next token refresh -- but this is Asana's general assertion, not a specific test case with documented before/after behavior on a live token; NOT independently verified against a dedicated 'permission revocation propagation' doc page in this research pass.
permission_shrink_test.verification_method: Attempt a get_task/get_project call against a resource the user no longer has access to using a still-valid (unexpired) token; expect a 403/permission-denied-shaped response consistent with Asana's standard errors model (docs/errors: HTTP status codes with a JSON errors array).
permission_shrink_test.gap: No dedicated official-docs page was found addressing token-vs-live-permission staleness windows explicitly; this scenario's expected outcome is inferred from the general access-control statement, not a directly confirmed test result.

multi_page_listing_test.scenario: List a resource collection (e.g. GET /tasks?project=X or MCP get_tasks) where the result set exceeds one page.
multi_page_listing_test.mechanism: REST: pass limit (1-100, default page size unspecified beyond 'a modest page size by default' per docs/rate-limits recommending limit=100); response includes next_page{offset, path, uri} when more results exist, null when exhausted (docs/pagination). Continue by passing the returned offset token on the next call. Offset tokens EXPIRE after some unspecified time ('an offset token will expire after some time, as data may have changed' -- exact TTL not documented).
multi_page_listing_test.hard_ceilings: Non-paginated ('legacy status') endpoints truncate around 1,000 objects and may time out; paginated endpoints cap each page at 100 objects (docs/pagination: 'able to page through all objects... up to 100 objects at a time').
multi_page_listing_test.mcp_equivalent: Several MCP tools state 'Supports pagination' (get_users, get_workspace_agents) without publishing the exact continuation-token parameter name in static docs -- must be confirmed via tools/list.
multi_page_listing_test.verification: Confirm next_page is non-null on a query known to exceed the page size, then confirm the follow-up call with that offset returns the next distinct slice and eventually a null next_page.

cross_workspace_access_denial_test.scenario: Attempt to read/write a resource (task/project) that belongs to a DIFFERENT workspace than the one the caller's token is scoped/authorized to.
cross_workspace_access_denial_test.mcp_specific_behavior: Because 'tokens are workspace-scoped' at MCP authorization time (docs/mcp-tools-reference), a call referencing a GID from another workspace should fail or return not-found/access-denied, since 'to work across multiple workspaces, you need separate sessions' -- explicitly documented, not inferred.
cross_workspace_access_denial_test.native_oauth_behavior: A standard OAuth/PAT token is not workspace-pinned the same way; cross-workspace denial there is governed purely by the authenticated user's actual Asana workspace membership -- if the user isn't a member of the target workspace, standard Asana access control (undocumented in granular test terms on the fetched pages, but consistent with the general 401/403 error model in docs/errors) applies.
cross_workspace_access_denial_test.verification: Issue a get_task call for a task_gid known to belong to workspace B while authenticated/scoped to workspace A; expect an access-denied or not-found class response per docs/errors' documented error-shape ({"errors":[{"message":...}]}) though the EXACT status code (403 vs 404) for this specific cross-workspace case was not independently confirmed on the fetched error-handling page in this session -- flagged as a gap.
cross_workspace_access_denial_test.gap: Exact HTTP status code returned specifically for a cross-workspace GID lookup was not directly observed in the fetched docs/errors excerpt (which showed 401 'Not Authorized' for a missing-auth-header example, not this scenario).

ambiguous_create_must_not_duplicate_test.scenario: A create_tasks (or create_project) call is retried after a network timeout/ambiguous response, risking a duplicate object.
ambiguous_create_must_not_duplicate_test.documented_facts: Asana's OWN rate-limits documentation explicitly flags this exact risk: 'Automatic retry typically applies to idempotent methods; if you retry POST creates yourself, make them idempotent so a retry can't create a duplicate.' (docs/rate-limits, step 1). CRITICALLY, no official Idempotency-Key header, client-supplied dedupe token, or natural-key uniqueness constraint for task/project creation was found in ANY of the pages fetched this session (createtask, createproject, mcp-tools-reference, rate-limits, errors).
ambiguous_create_must_not_duplicate_test.recommended_mitigation_not_officially_pr: Because Asana provides no built-in idempotency primitive for creates, the only implementable mitigation surfaced by the docs' own general guidance is client-side: (a) search for a pre-existing task/project with matching name+context via search_tasks/get_tasks or search_objects before creating, or (b) maintain a client-side request-id ledger and skip re-issuing a create whose prior attempt's outcome is unknown until confirmed via a read-back. This is Kiro Crew's own inferred mitigation strategy, not an Asana-documented feature -- must be explicitly labeled as such and not presented as an official Asana capability.
ambiguous_create_must_not_duplicate_test.verification: Issue a create_tasks call, kill the connection before the response is received, then re-issue the identical call; inspect whether two tasks with identical name+context now exist. Expected outcome per the ABSENCE of idempotency support: duplication is likely unless the caller has independently implemented the mitigation above.

contradictions.topic: V1 MCP server deprecation shutdown date
contradictions.detail: docs/integrating-with-asanas-mcp-server states the V1 Beta SSE server (https://mcp.asana.com/sse) 'is deprecated and will shut down on Wed 5 Aug 2026 (extended from the previous date 11 May 2026)'. However, two OTHER official pages fetched in the same session -- docs/using-asanas-mcp-server and docs/connecting-mcp-clients-to-asanas-v2-server -- both still state the shutdown date as plain '05/11/2026' with no mention of the extension. This is an internal inconsistency WITHIN Asana's own official documentation site, observed across three pages at the same observed_at timestamp (2026-09-14), not a Kiro Crew research error. Treat the extended date (5 Aug 2026) on the integrating-with-asanas-mcp-server page as more likely current since it explicitly narrates the extension, but flag the discrepancy to any implementer relying on the exact date.

The REST API (per the full API Reference sidebar fetched) exposes CRUD for dozens of resource types (custom fields, sections, dependencies, attachments upload/delete, portfolios, goals, tags, teams management, memberships, etc.), while the documented MCP Tools Reference exposes a much smaller curated set (roughly 18 read tools, 6 write tools, 3 interactive tools as of this snapshot). This is not a contradiction in the sense of conflicting statements, but a confirmed, real capability gap between the two surfaces that must not be papered over -- e.g. there is no MCP tool for deleting a project, updating an existing project's fields, managing custom field definitions, uploading attachments, or managing sections/dependencies as first-class operations (dependencies are folded into update_tasks; sections are folded into get_project).

Not a true contradiction, but worth flagging as apparent redundancy: get_user documented as usable with no identifier to mean 'the authenticated user', while get_me is a separate dedicated tool for the same authenticated-user case. Asana's own doc distinguishes them by convenience/specificity ('Use get_me when you need specific details... rather than just their GID'), so this is deliberate API design, not a documentation error.

gaps: Exact JSON input/output schemas for ALL MCP tools are NOT published in static documentation. Asana explicitly and repeatedly directs implementers to the live 'tools/list' MCP command as the sole authoritative schema source. Every MCP-sourced operation_id in this report inherits this gap.

No official Asana MCP server changelog entry or dated release note beyond the forum post 'New V2 MCP server now generally available!' (used only as a corroborating, non-authoritative signal, not cited as a primary source in the operations table) was independently fetched in full in this session; the forum is community/product-announcement space, not developers.asana.com API docs proper, so it was deliberately excluded from primary sourcing per the task's restriction to official docs.

No native idempotency-key or dedupe mechanism exists for ANY create (task, project, custom field, etc.) across both REST and MCP surfaces, confirmed by explicit absence across createtask, createproject, createcustomfield, mcp-tools-reference, and rate-limits pages, and by rate-limits.md's own explicit warning that retry-safety for POST creates is the CALLER's responsibility.

Explicit plan-tier gating for Portfolios, Goals, and Teams API access was not independently re-confirmed against a specific official docs statement in this research pass (only Custom Fields and Search Tasks were explicitly and directly confirmed as Premium-gated, and Workspace Events as Enterprise+/Service-Account-gated). Any claim of a hard plan gate for portfolios/goals/teams beyond what is stated here would be an inference, not a confirmed fact, and is deliberately NOT asserted.

No OAuth scope entry for 'Agents' (AI Teammates) or for 'Sections' was found in the fetched docs/oauth-scopes page's scope table, despite both having documented REST endpoints and/or MCP tools -- this may reflect an omission in Asana's own scope documentation, a folding under a broader scope, or a newer feature not yet reflected in that table. Flagged, not resolved.

Delete/attachment-upload parity at the MCP layer: MCP exposes get_attachments (read-only) with no corresponding create/delete attachment MCP tool, and no MCP tool for deleting a project or updating an existing project's fields was found, despite full REST support for both. Confirmed absent, not merely unverified.

Cross-workspace access-denial exact HTTP status code (403 vs 404) was not independently observed for the specific GID-belongs-to-another-workspace case; only a generic missing-auth-header 401 example was captured from docs/errors in this session.

Permission-shrink-while-token-still-valid propagation timing (immediate vs cached) is asserted by Asana only in general terms ('access is determined by the authenticated user's Asana permissions') without a dedicated test-case or staleness-window statement.

MCP list_workspaces / get_workspace as discrete tool names: not found in the published MCP Tools Reference table. Workspace selection for MCP appears to happen entirely at OAuth-authorization time (choosing a workspace during the consent flow), not via a runtime tool call -- this is inferred from the 'Tokens are workspace-scoped' statement and the absence of any workspace-listing tool in the table, and should be verified live via tools/list before an implementer assumes it is unavailable, since Asana explicitly states the tool set evolves over time.

operations.input_schema_summary: n/a (applies to every read/write API call)
operations.output_schema_summary: n/a
acceptance_preconditions: Sharing rules, field-level security, validation rules, Apex triggers, and Flow automation are enforced server-side on every API path (REST, Bulk, SOAP) exactly as in the UI -- there is no supported way to bypass them via API. Any integration design that assumes API access can skip validation/sharing is incorrect and must not be built that way.
operations.source_note: original category label from source research pass: 'governance_fact'; original effect field from source research pass (non-conforming, normalized): 'governance_fact'

flows: OAuth 2.0 Web-Server (Authorization Code) Flow with PKCE: 3-legged, user-facing, requires browser redirect and user login/consent. PKCE (code_verifier/code_challenge) applies specifically to this flow to protect the authorization code from interception, especially for public clients without a client secret.

JWT Bearer Flow: 2-legged, server-to-server, non-interactive. App signs a JWT with an RSA private key registered on the app; no authorization code/redirect exists in this flow, so PKCE does not and cannot apply.

Client Credentials Flow: 2-legged, server-to-server, non-interactive. Uses client_id/client_secret directly against the token endpoint; runs as a designated 'Run As' execution user with API Only User permission; no authorization code/redirect, so PKCE does not apply here either.
auth_facts.pkce_scope_statement: PKCE governs ONLY the user-facing OAuth 2.0 Web-Server (authorization code) flow. It is a mitigation for authorization-code interception during the browser redirect step. JWT-bearer and Client-Credentials flows are service-to-service by definition, have no redirect/authorization-code exchange, and therefore do not use or require PKCE. Do not describe PKCE as governing JWT-bearer or client-credentials.
auth_facts.terminology: 'External Client App' is Salesforce's current (post-2024) terminology and UI surface for what was previously called a 'Connected App'. Legacy Connected Apps continue to exist and function; new integrations are steered toward External Client Apps, which separate the OAuth policy configuration from the app's core definition.
auth_facts.my_domain_requirement: My Domain (a org-specific subdomain, e.g. yourorg.my.salesforce.com) is a mandatory precondition for modern OAuth flows and for many current API/login behaviors; legacy generic login endpoints are increasingly deprecated/restricted without My Domain enabled.
auth_facts.api_versioning: Every REST/Bulk/Tooling API endpoint is pinned to an explicit version segment in the URL path (e.g. /services/data/v62.0/...). Salesforce does not silently upgrade a caller's pinned version; callers must explicitly bump their version string to adopt new API behavior, and old pinned versions continue to be served per Salesforce's version-support policy.
auth_facts.server_side_enforcement: Sharing rules, field-level security, validation rules, Apex triggers, and Flow automation all fire identically for API-driven changes as for UI-driven changes. There is no API bypass switch for business logic enforcement.

scenario_preconditions: A sandbox (not production) org provisioned with at least 2-3 custom objects (with relationships/lookups to standard objects and to each other) to exercise describe, SOQL joins, and CRUD end-to-end.

A real write followed by an immediate read-back of the same record (create -> get by Id, or upsert by external id -> get) to confirm server-side field defaulting, validation rule side effects, and any Flow/trigger-populated fields are visible, not just trusting the write response.

A restricted-field-access-denial test: a test user/profile with FLS deliberately restricting one or more fields on the target object, then attempting to read/write that field via API, confirming the API returns the correct FLS-driven omission/error rather than silently succeeding.

A business-validation-error test: an object with an active validation rule that the payload deliberately violates, confirming the API surfaces the specific validation error message/fields rather than a generic failure.

A timeout-must-not-retry test: a scenario simulating client-side timeout on a CREATE call, confirming the calling system does not blindly re-POST the same create (which would duplicate the record) without deduplication logic (e.g. checking for an existing record via external id or idempotency key pattern first).
contradictions: The prompt's phrasing 'SOQL query with pagination (queryMore/nextRecordsUrl)' names two constructs from different API generations: queryMore belongs to the SOAP API; the REST API's equivalent pagination mechanism is nextRecordsUrl (returned when done=false). Only nextRecordsUrl is applicable to REST-based integrations; queryMore is not a REST API endpoint.

Community/official-adjacent sources indicate Bulk API 2.0 can report job state as 'JobComplete' before failedResults/successfulResults are fully populated for download -- callers should not treat state=JobComplete alone as proof that per-row result files are final and complete.

For guaranteed update-never-insert semantics against an external id (as opposed to native upsert's insert-or-update), the plain external-id PATCH endpoint is insufficient by itself per community guidance; a Composite request (lookup by external id, then explicit PATCH by internal Id) is the documented workaround.

Exact current synchronous row-limit threshold before Reports API forces asynchronous execution was not re-confirmed against a live official page this session.

acceptance_preconditions: Recording download_url/play_url values and any OAuth access/refresh tokens carry bearer-style access rights embedded in the URL or header value itself; these MUST NEVER be written to logs, error traces, or monitoring systems in plaintext. operations.source_note: original category label from source research pass: 'governance_fact'; original effect field from source research pass (non-conforming, normalized): 'governance_fact'

modes: User-level OAuth (3-legged, authorization_code grant): tied to one specific human user; requires browser redirect + consent; issues both access_token and refresh_token; token scope = that user's own Zoom permissions.

Server-to-Server OAuth (account_credentials grant): 2-legged, non-interactive; app authenticates with its own client_id/client_secret directly to the token endpoint plus account_id; issues only an access_token (NO refresh_token -- request a brand-new token on expiry); token scope = whatever scopes the account admin pre-authorized for that specific app in the Marketplace, representing an account/app-level service identity rather than any individual person.
auth_facts.token_lifetime: Both modes issue bearer access tokens valid for 3600 seconds (1 hour, reported as expires_in=3599 in practice).
auth_facts.uuid_encoding_quirk: Any Zoom meeting or webinar UUID that starts with a forward slash '/' or contains a double-slash '//' must be DOUBLE URL-encoded before being placed in a path segment (encode the raw UUID once, then URL-encode that already-encoded string again) -- a single encoding pass is insufficient and the API returns a 'meeting/webinar does not exist' style error (e.g. code 3001) otherwise. This affects past_meetings, past_webinars, recordings, and transcript/AI-companion endpoints that take a UUID path parameter.
auth_facts.secrets_handling: Recording download_url/play_url values embed short-lived signed access tokens as query parameters; OAuth access tokens and (for user-level flow) refresh tokens are bearer credentials. None of these must ever be written to logs, error messages, or monitoring/tracing systems in plaintext.

scenario_preconditions: A real, already-ended meeting fixture that has: cloud recording present (with recording_files of multiple types e.g. MP4/transcript), a completed participant list (past_meetings participants), and a generated AI meeting summary (meeting_summary) -- so read/detail/summary/participants can all be exercised against one consistent real object rather than four unrelated fixtures.

A webinar fixture (past, already-occurred) with registrants and participants populated, to exercise webinar list/detail/participants/registrants distinctly from the meeting-oriented endpoints, since webinars require a separate paid add-on and have their own endpoint family.

A license-tier-gated feature (e.g. Webinars add-on, Cloud Recording, or AI Companion/Meeting Summary) deliberately tested against an account/user WITHOUT that entitlement, confirming the API correctly returns a blocked/forbidden/feature-not-enabled response rather than silently succeeding or returning fabricated/empty-but-200 data that could be mistaken for 'feature works, just no data yet'.
contradictions: Devforum evidence suggests AI Companion transcript/summary retrieval works reliably via API for admin-role tokens but has been reported unreliable for standard non-admin user-role tokens on some accounts -- this role-based access behavior appears account-specific/support-dependent rather than a single universally documented rule, and should be verified against the specific target account rather than assumed.

The feature branding/licensing language for 'Meeting Summary with AI Companion' varies across current support pages (one referencing BAA-linked availability for healthcare-context customers, another referencing general account-level enable/disable toggles) -- these are not necessarily contradictory (they may describe different account types) but were not reconciled into one single authoritative current statement during this session and should be treated as requiring live verification against the specific target account's entitlements.
gaps: AI-generated meeting TEMPLATES (as distinct from meeting summaries) were not confirmed as a documented current public REST API surface during this session's research; only the meeting_summary/meeting_summaries family of endpoints was confirmed via search of official docs and changelog references. This should be treated as unconfirmed rather than asserted.

A distinct, current, direct REST 'archive a recording' POST endpoint (separate from the webhook-driven Recording Archiving add-on flow) could not be confirmed against a live-rendered official docs page in this session.

Exact current minimum license/add-on tier wording for 'Meeting Summary with AI Companion' (e.g., whether it is now bundled into a specific Zoom Workplace Pro tier vs requiring a separate Custom AI Companion paid add-on) could not be pinned to one single authoritative current statement; treat as requiring live re-verification against Zoom's current pricing/licensing page before building a hard tier-gate check.

operations.input_schema_summary: { drive_item_ref, edit_spec: {part_path: e.g. 'word/document.xml'|'ppt/slides/slide3.xml', operation: 'replace_text'|'replace_paragraph'|'append', payload}, mode: 'in_place_update'|'save_as_new_file', if_match_etag?: string }
operations.output_schema_summary: { id, name, webUrl, eTag (new), mode_applied, previousETag? }
operations.region_edition_license: Same deployment coverage as driveItem content endpoint (Global, GCC High, DoD, China-21Vianet)
operations.endpoint: No native Graph endpoint for targeted part edits. Composite operation: (1) GET .../content to download, (2) unzip and rewrite the specific OOXML part (document.xml / slideN.xml / sheetN.xml) locally while preserving all other parts, relationships (.rels), and [Content_Types].xml unchanged, (3) rezip, (4) PUT .../content (in_place_update, same item id) or PUT .../{parent-id}:/{new-filename}:/content (save_as_new_file, new item).
operations.idempotency_recovery: in_place_update is NOT safe to blind-retry: use If-Match header with the eTag read at step 1 (confirmed pattern: 'If you provide the header with a valid etag... the request will only complete successfully if the current state matches; otherwise 412 Precondition Failed' -- stackoverflow.com/questions/45942504, corroborated by MS Q&A on conflictBehavior/if-match). On 412, re-download, re-apply edit against the new content, retry once. save_as_new_file avoids the concurrency hazard entirely by never touching the original item.
contradictions: None -- explicitly the 'rewrite-and-reupload' pattern independently confirmed by a third-party source (scalekit.com: 'The Graph path is to download the file, edit it locally with a library, then re-upload. Surgical paragraph and run edits happen in your code, not in the API') and Microsoft's own Q&A guidance pointing to third-party libraries like Aspose for this exact gap.
operations.acceptance_preconditions: Original file must round-trip through unzip/rezip without corrupting sibling parts (relationships, styles, media, custom XML, content types); mode selection (in_place vs save_as_new) must be explicit per call, defaulting to save_as_new_file for safety unless caller opts into in_place_update with etag guard.
gaps: This is inherently fragile compared to a real content API: any OOXML part not touched must still be repacked byte-correctly enough for Word/PowerPoint/Excel to reopen it; a naive full-document-tree serialization can lose formatting nuances (run properties, revision tracking) not represented in a simplified read/write schema. Requires the layout/chart/image roundtrip fixture described below.
